t0x: Dysfunctional Family Roles: The Parts We Play to Survive
t1x: When a family lives with ongoing stress (addiction, anger, illness, divorce, a harsh or absent parent), children unconsciously take on roles that keep the system going: the Hero who makes the family look good, the Scapegoat who carries the blame, the Lost Child who disappears, the Mascot who lightens the mood, the Caretaker who holds everyone together, and the Golden Child who carries the parents' hopes. Each role protects the child, and each has a cost that follows them into adult life.

t36x: God sets the solitary in families (Psalm 68:6), and He knows each child by name. Joseph was the favoured son and then the scapegoat, sold by jealous brothers, yet God redeemed the family story: "Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50:20). In Christ we are adopted sons and daughters (Galatians 4:7), loved for who we are, not for the part we play.
t37x: In hard families, children often play a part, like the helper, the joker or the one who gets blamed, to cope. You can step out of that part.
t39x: Research on parenting describes two big ingredients: warmth (love, responsiveness, connection) and structure (limits, expectations, follow-through). Mix them and you get four styles: Authoritative (warm and firm), Authoritarian (firm but cold), Permissive (warm but no limits) and Uninvolved (neither warmth nor structure). Children thrive best with warmth and structure together.

t75x: Over-Involved Parenting: Helicopter, Snowplough and Tiger
t76x: Modern parents often love by doing too much: hovering over every moment (helicopter), clearing every obstacle out of the way (snowplough or lawnmower), pushing relentlessly for achievement (tiger), protecting from all risk (bubble-wrap), or serving every need (concierge). It usually comes from love and anxiety, but it can leave children anxious, dependent, entitled or afraid to fail.

t314x: Anita, the family hero who could never rest
t315x: Anita, 38, the eldest daughter and a hospital manager in Chennai
t316x: Anita was top of her class, paid her siblings' fees and organised every family crisis. At work she said yes to everything. At 38 she collapsed with exhaustion, yet still felt she had never done enough.
t317x: Her father drank and her mother was often ill. As the eldest, Anita learned that if she was perfect and in control, the family would survive and look respectable. Her worth became tied to achieving and rescuing.
t318x: Her doctor ordered rest, and a counsellor asked, "Who were you allowed to be as a child?" Anita realised she had been the family Hero, and she had never been allowed to be a child.
t319x: Mapped her family roles and saw the pattern
